title.narrative: Tautua: Samoa Human Development and Social Inclusion

description.narrative: The Tautua - Human Development for All program for Samoa builds on Australia's investments across human development sectors. It provides institutional strengthening support to Government and the community sector to improve the quality and inclusiveness of service delivery in relation to health, education, gender equality and disability inclusion. It focuses on four critical social issues: reducing non-communicable diseases; reversing stagnated leaning outcomes; reducing the vulnerability of those whose rights to exercise a choice and whose personal safety are threatened; and overcoming barriers to inclusive communities.

title.narrative: Samoa Human Development and Social Inclusion Program Investment Concept Note
Samoa Human Development and Social Inclusion Program Investment Concept Note

description.narrative: Australia, through the Tautua: Human Development facility: ‍ -is supporting employment of an international pathologist within Samoa’s Ministry of Health. Concurrently, a local pathologist-in-training is undertaking a post graduate diploma to ensure sustainability and future local provision of this critical service. This has enabled 653 histology, 210 cytology and 399 haematology tests, allowing for timely results for early diagnosis and prevention of non-communicable diseases. ‍ -procured mini-servers for seven rural district hospitals across Samoa, allowing them to access and safely store patient information onsite, and enabling physicians at the two main referral hospitals more appropriate and timely access to patient information. ‍ -supported the completion of Samoa's first National Cancer Control Policy, providing strategic guidance for planning and implementation of cancer control programs, supporting resource allocation and clearer pathway for diagnosis, referral and treatment, and promoting coordination and collaboration between stakeholders, strengthening coordination of messaging to increase awareness of cancer risks.

The Samoa Health System Strengthening Performance for Results (PforR) program, a World Bank-Australia-New Zealand co-funded program, supported the integration of non-communicable disease-related (NCD) data into the Ministry of Health's centralised e-health information system. PforR focuses on strengthening primary health care through NCD community screening and school health promotion programs to curb the rise of NCDs. The integrated components enable medical practitioners across the country to have better access to up-to-date patient medical records allowing for timely detection, referral and treatment for people at risk of or living with NCDs, regardless of where they present to a medical facility.

The Tautua – Human Development for All partnership supported the development of an asset register module in collaboration with the Australia-based company Beyond Essential Systems, for the registration of Ministry of Health (MoH) capital assets. The MoH previously had to rely on two separate registers from the former Ministry of Health and National Health Services that lacked integration, limiting effective maintenance, planning and resource allocation. In June 2024, the new register was launched streamlining inventory tracking, and enabling timely maintenance, replacement and distribution of assets across public health facilities. This supported better access to essential medical equipment and resources for patient management and treatment.

The Tautua – Human Development for All partnership, is supporting the Samoa Victim Support Group (SVSG), a civil society organization mandated to support victims of gender-based violence. Australia supported a Helpline call support service for women experiencing violence, a rehabilitation program for perpetrators, as well as village representative training and referral program. Two dedicated staff supported by Tautua have improved operational efficiency and provided 24-hour assistance for the SVSG helpline. The SVSG provided services to 386 beneficiaries, 187 of which were assisted through the helpline. During the reporting year, SVSG was provided with capacity building sessions which address child protection, social safeguards, as well as GEDSI to improve internal processes and ensure better alignment with Australia’s DO NO HARM and LEAVE NO ONE BEHIND principles.

The Tautua: Human Development program supported the engagement of two helpline operators for the Samoa Victim Support Group, a civil society organization mandated to support victims of gender-based violence. The two dedicated staff have supported operational efficiency and provided 24-hour assistance for the SVSG Helpline. For the reporting period, a total of 2,493 incidences of services were provided to survivors of SGBV of which 2,198 were assisted through the Helpline Services. The helpline has recently expanded its focus to mental health and suicide tendencies in response to the recent closure of a civil society focusing on suicide. Additionally, SVSG was supported through trainings on child protection, social safeguarding and gender and disability mainstreaming, to ensure alignment with Australian programming principles of 'dp no harm' and 'leave no one behind.'

The development of the Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) for Tobacco Control and the E-cigarette Regulations through the Australia-Samoa Tautua partnership contribute to the alignment of Samoa's Tobacco Control Act to the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control and the effective management of non-communicable diseases (NCDs). While the SOP ensures consistent enforcement, regulatory oversight and compliance monitoring through improved coordination with other relevant sectors, the E-cigarette Regulations bridges the regulatory gaps in the Tobacco Control Act to address the increasing use of e-cigarettes, an emerging issue in the management of NCDs. Both documents align with Samoa's first National Cancer Control policy also developed with Tautua support, which provides a structured framework for the prevention, detection, referral and treatment of cancer.

Through the Tautua – Human Development for All partnership, Australia continued to fund an international pathologist to support the Ministry of Health (MoH) in the absence of a qualified local pathologist. This role provides clinical oversight and leadership that has improved quality and standards in pathology services, while also providing capacity building and mentoring for the general laboratory staff and technicians. This technical advisory role enabled the timely completion of 1,020 histology and 320 cytology tests between January and October 2024 . In the absence of a pathologist, MoH would be reliant on samples being sent overseas for testing, resulting in higher costs, delayed results, referrals and treatment of patients. This role is expected to continue for the next two years, while the pathologist-in-training completes her fellowship program in 2025 and subsequently a Master of Pathology in 2026 through the Australia Awards program, ensuring the sustainability of pathology services for the health sector.

Through the Tautua – Human Development for All partnership, five capacity gaps in clinical specialist areas are being addressed through professional development opportunities. Local practitioners will upskill through Postgraduate diploma courses at the Fiji National University over three years. The first to be completed in 2024 is the Postgraduate Diploma in Pathology to fill a critical personnel gap in country. The four remaining areas are intensive care – currently in progress, emergency nursing, mental health and peri-operative – approved and expected to be undertaken in the next two years of the program, minimizing staff shortages for the Ministry of Health and improving access to essential services.

Under the Tautua: Human Development for All facility for the reporting period, a total of 2,346 women were able to access family planning and sexual and reproductive health services through the Samoa Family Health Association (SFHA) clinics, 1,947 of whom were reached through mobile clinics to communities. In comparison, only 174 women were able to access static and mobile clinics within the September 2022-June 2023 period. The direct grant support provided to SFHA includes the hire of a nurse to conduct mobile clinics for remote villages on the island of Savaii. A most significant story documented by a client of SFHA reflects her appreciation for the SFHA in helping her plan the frequency of her pregnancies through advice and contraceptives provided through their mobile services. Additionally, it has increased her awareness of risks of unplanned pregnancies and different types of contraceptives to her health and well-being.
